transcript:
This is NPR News now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from the NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Investors on Wall Street dumped artificial intelligence stocks this week, dragging the
broader market down with them.
The NASDAQ composite fell 10 percent for the week, wiping out its gains for the year.
The slide has investors wondering whether the AI bubble is starting to burst.
NPR's Rafi El-Nam reports.
I think what we are seeing here is the combination of fears that have been building up for weeks,
and that even Anthropics IPO was able to tamp down those anxieties.
First, back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in
over three years.
That's a big challenge because borrowing gets more expensive, and AI companies still need
to borrow billions of dollars to do things like building out data centers.
That's NPR's Rafi El-Nam reporting.
President Trump is threatening to hit U.S. tech companies with what he calls a tremendous
tax if they build AI data centers overseas.
Trump says building more data centers at home is critical to winning the AI race.
Democrats, who are set to regain control of Congress in January, have pledged to put tighter
limits on the facilities, which use large amounts of electricity.
A judge has ruled that the Trump administration's plan to overhaul funding for homelessness
programs is unlawful, and PR's Jennifer Ludden reports that HUD wants to shift money away
from programs that support permanent housing.
The decision is the latest setback for the Trump administration's push to fund more transitional
housing with mandated treatment for addiction.
The ruling found that doing so would exceed HUD's authority and go against requirements
set by Congress.
The judge also struck down a restriction on so-called harm reduction efforts, like offering
clean needle exchanges for drug users.
Democratic-led states and homeless advocacy groups brought the suit and argued that long-term
housing without preconditions has a long track record of success.
HUD Secretary Scott Turner disputes that claim and told Reuters the agency reserves the right
to appeal.
The court ruling comes just over a week before the deadline, when local providers must apply
for federal grants.
Jennifer Ludden in PR News, Washington.
A storm forming off the east coast of Florida is expected to track northeast this weekend.
Forecasters say it could strengthen into a tropical or subtropical storm.
Meteorologist David Roth with the Weather Prediction Center says the rain will spread
into Georgia and the Carolinas.
So, the forecast is for areas of one to two inches of rain across portions of Georgia
and coastal South Carolina, with local maxima probably in the range of four inches, so much
lower than what Florida has had, but still wet.
The National Hurricane Center says strong gusts and dangerous surf are possible along
parts of the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Rescue crews are navigating flooded streets in Florida after days of heavy rain along
the state's Atlantic coast.
That rain is eased in the central part of the state, but forecasters say the St. Johns
River could keep rising for several more days.
There's a new effort underway in northern Minnesota to help bring back an ancient fish,
Minnesota Public Radio's Dan Crocker reports on the giant Lake Sturgeon.
Sturgeon are enormous fish that can live well over 100 years.
They were wiped out from the St. Louis River in the mid-1900s.
For decades, biologists have worked to bring them back.
Miranda Riney with the Great Lakes Aquarium says this new approach raises baby sturgeon
directly in water from the river.
The sturgeon imprint on the water they're raised on within the first 30 to 45 days of
their life, and that cues them of where to return to spawn.
Earlier this month, hundreds of seven-inch-long sturgeon were released into the river.
Have a good life, little buddies!
The goal is to make their populations self-sustaining.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Crocker in Duluth.
A mathematician at Anthropic says the company's AI chatbot Claude may have helped him solve
one of math's biggest mysteries.
It's called the Riemann hypothesis, and it deals with how prime numbers are spread out.
The problem has stumped mathematicians since 1859.
The researcher says he believes they found proof and credits Claude with much of the work
near the end.
So far, the proposed proof has not been independently verified.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Wall Street dumps AI stocks, NASDAQ falls 10 percent for the week, erasing year's gains
Trump threatens U.S. tech companies with tremendous tax over overseas AI data centers
Judge rules Trump administration's homelessness funding overhaul unlawful, HUD plans to appeal
Storm off Florida's east coast expected to track northeast, bringing rain to Georgia and Carolinas
Rescue crews navigate flooded Florida streets after heavy Atlantic coast rain; St. Johns River rising
Northern Minnesota effort releases hundreds of lake sturgeon into St. Louis River to restore population
Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped him find proof of Riemann hypothesis, unverified
